title: the Rudram
hook: the Rudram is built out of one small word, namah, said again and again until the bowing becomes the rhythm

segments.voice: Yesterday the Rudram pointed at the copper-red sun and said the cowherds have seen him. Did you look up during an errand? Today closes the week. Day one thousand one hundred forty-eight.
screen: `THE COWHERDS HAVE SEEN HIM.` · `THE WEEK CLOSES.`

segments.voice: Namo. Namah. Namo. Namah. Sit near people chanting the Rudram, and that's the sound that keeps coming around, like a drumbeat under the melody. The names change. The images change. A warrior, a tree, a river, a thief. But again and again the line lands on the same small word. If you don't know a word of Sanskrit, you'll still hear it. Today we stop on that one word, and look back at a week that kept bowing.
screen: `NAMO. NAMAH. NAMO.` → `A DRUMBEAT UNDER THE MELODY.` → `ONE SMALL WORD.`

segments.voice: Namah means a bow, homage, a gesture of honor. It's the same word inside namaste, the greeting: a bow to you. In the Rudram, line after line is built the same way. Namah, then a name or a description of Rudra, and often a little word, cha, which means and. A bow to this one, and to that one. And to this, and to that. Tradition calls this first part of the Rudram the Namakam, the part made of namah. Why build a hymn that way? Here's one way to hear it. Much of the hymn is a list. It names Rudra in one place, then another, then another, until it seems there's nowhere he isn't. But a list alone could be just information. The bow turns every item into a meeting. Each time the chanter says namah, they don't just mention Rudra in a river or a field. They greet him there. And the repetition does something to the one chanting. Bow once and it's a gesture. Bow over and over, and bowing starts to become the way you stand. Now look back at this week. It began in the Shiva Sutras with a dancer who never forgets who's dancing. Then the teacher as the way. Then the snap of waking, named Bhairava. Then talk that becomes japa. Then the Rudram began: a bow to Rudra's anger and a plea to unstring the bow. Then the sun crossing the sky, seen by cowherds. A week of noticing, ending in one plain word that does the noticing out loud. Namah. I see you there, and I bow.
screen: `NAMAH — A BOW.` · `A BOW TO THIS, AND TO THAT.` · `A LIST BECOMES A MEETING.` · `A WEEK OF NOTICING.` · then, large: `I SEE YOU THERE, AND I BOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small inward bow. Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. With your eyes open, let them rest on one thing in the room. On the out-breath, make a tiny inward bow toward it. Not a physical one, unless you want to. Just a nod of honor, inside. Then let the eyes move to the next thing, and bow again. The chair. The window. Your own hands. If you pray, you can say namah, silently, with each one. The bell holds the time.
The Rudram. Today's word inside it: namah, a bow, said again and again until the hymn becomes a long greeting.
Your line: the Rudram. Today, when you greet someone, let the hello be a small bow on the inside. Day one thousand one hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: The Rudram is chanted in Vedic Sanskrit, with the namah lines carrying its rhythm; in temple abhishekam and in group chanting, people often recite it together, and the word namah is heard throughout.

original.note: Sanskrit: a bow, homage. the word that carries the rhythm of the Rudram's Namakam.

trapdoor: what you thought: a word that sounds like part of namaste.
what it means: a bow of homage, repeated through the Rudram until the whole hymn becomes a greeting.
what a scholar hears: the Namakam of Taittiriya Samhita 4.5, its lines built on namah with the dative and paired with cha, as in namo ... cha ... cha.
